10.0.big: Every one of your trillions of cells came from one fertilized egg dividing again and again. Cell division builds bodies, repairs them, and is how single cells reproduce.
points: Multicellular organisms divide cells to grow, to maintain, and to repair tissue. Skin and blood cells are replaced all the time.
Cell division is tightly controlled. When the controls fail, the result can be cancer.
Most nerve cells don't divide, which is why nerve damage is so hard to heal.

10.1.big: A cell's DNA (its genome) is packed into chromosomes. Before a cell divides, each chromosome is copied so both new cells get a full set.
points: Prokaryotes have one circular chromosome (in the nucleoid). Eukaryotes have several linear chromosomes in a nucleus.
Human body (somatic) cells are diploid (2n = 46): two sets, one from each parent. Gametes (egg and sperm) are haploid (n = 23).
Homologous chromosomes are a matched pair: same genes in the same places (loci), but possibly different versions.
Genes code for proteins that produce traits (like blood type A, B or O).
Packing: DNA wraps around histone proteins to make nucleosomes ("beads on a string"), which coil and fold again and again. Two meters of DNA fit in a tiny nucleus.
After copying, a chromosome is two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere.

10.2.big: The cell cycle is a long prep phase (interphase), then the dividing phase: mitosis (splitting the nucleus) and cytokinesis (splitting the cell).
points: Interphase (most of the cell's life): G1, grow and stock up; S, copy the DNA; G2, final prep and make proteins for division.
Prophase: chromosomes condense, the nuclear envelope breaks up, and the spindle starts forming.
Prometaphase: spindle fibers grab each chromatid at its kinetochore.
Metaphase: chromosomes line up in the middle (the metaphase plate).
Anaphase: sister chromatids are pulled apart to opposite poles.
Telophase: new nuclei form around each set and the chromosomes relax.
Cytokinesis: animal cells pinch in (a cleavage furrow made by an actin ring). Plant cells build a cell plate that becomes the new wall.
G0: cells that aren't dividing, like mature nerve and heart cells, rest here.
10.2.tip: Order of mitosis: PPMAT, "Please Pass Me A Taco": Prophase, Prometaphase, Metaphase (Middle), Anaphase (Apart), Telophase (Two nuclei).

10.3.big: The cell cycle has checkpoints, like quality-control stops, and molecules that either push the cycle forward or hit the brakes.
points: G1 checkpoint: big enough? Enough energy? DNA undamaged? Growth factors are what push a cell past it.
G2 checkpoint: was all the DNA copied correctly?
M checkpoint (in metaphase): is every chromatid attached to the spindle? Anaphase can't be undone, so it waits.
Positive regulators (the gas pedal): cyclins pair with Cdks (cyclin-dependent kinases), which add phosphates to proteins that move the cycle forward.

Negative regulators (the brakes): p53 spots damaged DNA, halts the cycle, calls in repair, and triggers apoptosis if the damage can't be fixed. p21 blocks Cdks. Rb holds the cycle until the cell is big enough.

10.4.big: Cancer is cell division out of control, caused by mutations in the genes that run the cell cycle.
points: Proto-oncogenes are normal "gas pedal" genes. A mutation can turn one into an oncogene, a gas pedal stuck down.
Tumor suppressor genes (like p53, p21 and Rb) are the brakes. Mutations that break them let damaged cells keep dividing.
Over half of human tumors have a broken p53.
Damaged cells pile up more mutations each time they divide, and eventually all the checkpoints fail and a tumor forms.
HPV makes a protein (E6) that marks p53 for destruction, which is how it can lead to cervical cancer.
10.4.tip: Cancer usually needs both: a stuck gas pedal (oncogene) and broken brakes (tumor suppressor).

10.5.big: Bacteria divide by binary fission: copy the single circular chromosome, pull the copies apart, and split in two. No mitosis needed.
points: Copying starts at one spot (the origin) and goes both ways around the loop.
There's no nucleus, so there's no karyokinesis and no mitotic spindle. The growing cell membrane helps pull the copies apart.
A ring of FtsZ protein directs the building of a septum that splits the cell.
FtsZ is related to tubulin, the protein that builds our mitotic spindle, which is evidence of shared ancestry.

1.why: Diploid is two sets of chromosomes, and haploid is one, so diploid is twice as many.

2.why: DNA first wraps around histone proteins to form nucleosomes.

3.why: Genes, inherited from both parents, determine traits.

4.why: Two identical copies held together at the centromere are sister chromatids.

5.why: DNA is copied in the S (synthesis) phase of interphase.

6.why: Sister chromatids separate during anaphase of mitosis, not during interphase.

7.why: Spindle fibers attach to kinetochores in prometaphase.

8.why: Golgi vesicles fuse into a cell plate, which becomes the new cell wall.

9.why: S phase is when DNA is copied, so blocking it means no DNA replication.

10.why: Outside signals like growth factors matter most at the G1 checkpoint, where the cell decides whether to divide at all.

11.why: The M checkpoint holds the cell in metaphase, so anaphase can't start until every chromatid is attached.

12.why: Cdks are kinases: once activated by cyclin, they phosphorylate other proteins.

13.why: p53 can trigger apoptosis when DNA damage can't be repaired.

14.why: The G2 checkpoint mainly checks that DNA replication was complete and accurate.

15.why: A change in a gene's nucleotide sequence is a gene mutation.

16.why: E6 binds p53 and marks it for destruction, removing the cell's brake.

17.why: Normal "gas pedal" genes are proto-oncogenes. They become oncogenes only when mutated.

18.why: p21 is made when p53 rises, and it blocks Cdk/cyclin activity.

19.why: There's no nucleus to divide, so there's no karyokinesis (mitosis).

20.why: That's false: bacteria don't have a mitotic spindle. The other statements are true.

21.why: FtsZ directs the building of the septum, which becomes the new walls.

22.why: Somatic cells are diploid with 46 chromosomes. Gametes are haploid with half as many (23).

23.why: DNA wraps around proteins (histones) into nucleosomes, which coil and fold into a much more compact form.

24.why: G<sub>1</sub>: grow and prepare. S: copy the DNA. G<sub>2</sub>: copy organelles and take down the cytoskeleton to get ready for mitosis.

25.why: These drugs attack the mitotic spindle. Without working spindle fibers, chromosomes can't line up or separate, so division stalls (and damaged cells may die).

26.why: With the drug, fewer cells are in G<sub>1</sub> (53% → 38%) and many more pile up in S (20% → 46%), so cells move out of G<sub>1</sub> faster and get stuck in S.

27.why: G<sub>1</sub>: enough reserves for S phase (plus size and DNA damage). G<sub>2</sub>: was the new DNA copied correctly? M: are the spindle fibers attached to every kinetochore?

28.why: Positive regulators push the cycle forward. Negative regulators stop it until problems are fixed.

29.why: The M checkpoint checks that sister chromatids are attached to the spindle. If it fails, chromosomes can be split wrongly (nondisjunction).

30.why: p53 checks DNA quality, calls in repair enzymes, and triggers apoptosis. A faulty p53 loses all three.

31.why: Killing a cell with unfixable DNA damage stops it from passing on mutations and making faulty proteins, which protects the whole body.

32.why: Both copy the DNA, separate the copies, and divide the cytoplasm.

33.why: FtsZ directs the building of the septum.

34.why: A karyotype of 46 chromosomes in pairs means a eukaryotic, diploid cell. Prokaryotes have one circular chromosome.

35.why: Eukaryotic DNA wraps around histones into nucleosomes and forms linear chromosomes. Prokaryotes have a single loop.

36.why: That's the false one: homologous chromosomes carry the same genes in the same places. They come from different parents and may differ slightly in sequence.

37.why: Down syndrome is an extra copy of chromosome 21.

39.why: Cells pile up in S phase, where DNA is copied, so the drug most likely interferes with DNA replication.

40.why: Sample B has twice the DNA of sample A: the cells have copied their DNA (S phase) but haven't divided yet.

41.why: CHK2 activates p53, p53 makes p21, and p21 holds the cycle until things are fixed. Then the cycle moves on.

42.why: The diagram's inhibition line runs from active Cdk4 back to the cyclin D1/Cdk4 complex, so that's what's under negative feedback.

43.why: The group with working p53 survives longer with fewer recurrences, so functional p53 helps against cancer.
